blocks.text: The eyes of doves are attributed to the bride in Cant. I, 15. and IV, 1., and to the bridegroom as well in Cant. V, 12.; that is, eyes that are pure, lovely, simple, and finally chaste. This last is what the Hebrews chiefly understand here, because the dove looks only to its mate and does not [II, 537] cast its eyes on any other. Rabbi Selomo: משמכרת את בן זוגה אונה מניחתו שיזדווג לאחר, After she has been betrothed to her mate, she does not delight in being joined to another. And Aben Ezra: מנהג בני יונה שלא להתחבר אלא עם זוגה שלה, Doves are not accustomed to associate with any other than their own mate. Aelian teaches the same of the wood pigeon in Hist. book 3, ch. 44, and then says: Ἐὰν δὲ ἐποφθαλμιάσωσιν ἑτέροις, περιέρχονται αὐτοὺς οἱ λοιποὶ, καὶ τὸν μὲν ἄῤῥενα οἱ ὁμογενεῖς διασπῶσιν, αἱ θήλειαι δὲ τὸν θῆλυν [Ean de epophthalmiasōsin heterois, perierchontai autous hoi loipoi, kai ton men arrena hoi homogeneis diaspōsin, hai thēleiai de ton thēlyn]; But if they cast lustful eyes on others, the rest surround them, and the males tear the male to pieces, the females the female. Note here that the verb ἐποφθαλμιᾶν [epophthalmian] is used of a lustful look, because the eyes are the leaders in love, and ἐκ τοῦ ὁρᾷν γίνεται ἐρᾷν [ek tou horan ginetai eran]. Hence John ^{a)} speaks of Ἡ ἐπιθυμία τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν [Hē epithymia tōn ophthalmōn], and Peter ^{b)} of ὀφθαλμοὺς ἔχοντες μεστοὺς μοιχαλίδος [ophthalmous echontes mestous moichalidos]. David ^{c)}, having learned this to his own cost, earnestly asked God to turn his eyes away so that they should not behold vanity. And Job ^{d)} made a covenant with them that they should not look upon a virgin. The interpreters inquire anxiously what these words refer to in Cant. V, 12.: His eyes (the bridegroom's) are like (the eyes) of doves by the streams of waters, washed in milk, dwelling by the fullness. I think the sacred writer had only this in view: that doves have livelier eyes by the waters, because they prefer to live near them. Accordingly Varro (De re rustica, book 3, chapter 7), in his description of the dovecote, τῆς περιστεροφείου [tēs peristeropheiou], says: There should be pure water flowing in, from which they can both drink and bathe; for these birds are very clean. And they are described not only as by the waters but also as by the fullness (supply "of the waters", as Scripture repeatedly speaks ^{e)} of the fullness of the sea), that is, by places where waters gush forth and come up close to the top of the banks, so that they are easy to drink from. The same doves are said to be washed in milk, that is, very white, as if things washed in milk became white, as things washed in ink become black. Compare Job. IX, 30.: If I wash myself with snow water, and cleanse my hands with soap. Far-fetched, and found nowhere else so far as I know, is the view of Gregory on the Canticle, chapter 5, that doves sit beside streams so that they may see in the water the shadow of birds flying overhead, and by throwing themselves upon it may thus escape the talons of birds of prey. But this seems to have been taken in part from the story of a certain bird which in Arabic is called خاطف ظله [khāṭif ẓillihi] chatipho-dhillihi, as if to say snatcher of its own shadow, because اذا راي ظله في الما اقبل اليه ليخطفه [idhā rāy ẓillahu fī al-mā aqbala ilayhi li-yakhṭafahu], when it sees its shadow in the water, it approaches it in order to snatch it. So Alcamus. In Damir it is called otherwise: [col. 12] قرلا [qirlā] koralla, a Persian word; رفراف [rafrāf] riphraph, from the fluttering of its wings; and [II, 538] ملاعب ظله [mulāʿib ẓillihi] mulaibo dhillihi, playing with its shadow. It is asserted to be في جنس العصافير [fī jins al-ʿaṣāfīr] of the kind of sparrows, or small birds. It is therefore not the jackdaw, which I once thought it was, because Tzetzes says of jackdaws in Chiliad 4, Hist. 119:

— εἴπερ χέεις ἔλαιον ἔν τινι λεκανίσκῃ, Πρὸς τὴν σκιὰν τὴν ἑαυτῶν τοὺς κολοιοὺς κρατήσῃς. Ναρκίσσους ἄλλους Λάκωνας ὄντας τῶν φιλοσκίων. [— eiper cheeis elaion en tini lekaniskē, Pros tēn skian tēn heautōn tous koloious kratēsēs. Narkissous allous Lakōnas ontas tōn philoskiōn.]

If you pour oil into a small basin, you will hold the jackdaws fast at their own shadow, as if they were Laconian Narcissi, of those who love their own shadow. Note in passing that Narcissus was not a Laconian but a Boeotian, as Ovid, Metam. book 3, Fab. 5, Conon, Hist. 24, Strabo, book 9, Hyginus, Fab. 271, Pausanias in the Boeotica, Claudian, book 2 de raptu, and countless others attest. Yet Tzetzes makes him a Laconian both here and in Chil. 1, Hist. 9, as if he were a countryman of Hyacinthus, with whom he compares him in Hist. 11. This μνημονικὸν σφάλμα [mnēmonikon sphalma] is not to be tolerated in a man who, in that very passage, boasts thus:
Οὐδὲ γὰρ μνημονέστερον τοῦ Τζέτζου Θεὸς ἄλλον Ἄνδρα τῶν πρίν τε, καὶ τῶν νῦν ἐξέφηνεν ἐν βίῳ. [Oude gar mnēmonesteron tou Tzetzou Theos allon Andra tōn prin te, kai tōn nyn exephēnen en biō.]
